nameStory: The Common Gull gets its straightforward name from being one of the most widespread and frequently seen gulls across northern regions of Europe and Asia. Despite its name suggesting it's ordinary, this gull was once lumped together with the Short-billed Gull and collectively called the 'Mew Gull' because of their distinctive mewing call that sounds quite different from the harsh cries of larger gulls.
description: The Common Gull is a medium-sized seabird that's smaller than the familiar Herring Gull but larger than a Ring-billed Gull. It has the classic gull appearance with clean white plumage on the head and body, pale gray wings and back, and bright yellow-green legs and bill. This species breeds across cool northern regions from Iceland to Russia, migrating south in winter to warmer coastal areas. In New England, it's an uncommon but regular winter visitor along our coasts.

idTips.label: Bill Color and Shape
idTips.description: Look for a bright yellow-green bill that's thinner and more delicate than a Herring Gull's hefty orange bill, with no red spot on the lower mandible

idTips.label: Leg Color
idTips.description: The legs are the same yellow-green color as the bill, creating a coordinated look that's quite different from the pink legs of Herring Gulls

idTips.label: Overall Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more compact than Herring Gulls, with a rounder head and gentler expression that gives it an almost dove-like appearance

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: The wingtips show more white than black compared to Herring Gulls, creating a cleaner, less contrasted pattern when the wings are folded or spread

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Makes a distinctive mewing call that's higher-pitched and more musical than the harsh laughing calls of larger gulls

habitat: Along New England's coastline, Common Gulls prefer rocky shores, harbors, and coastal mudflats where they forage for small fish, marine worms, and crustaceans. They're often found mixed in with flocks of more common gulls at fishing ports, beaches, and tidal pools. Unlike some larger gulls, they tend to avoid heavily developed areas and garbage dumps, preferring cleaner marine environments.

seasonality.spring: Most Common Gulls are departing New England waters by late March, heading north to their breeding grounds. Any birds seen in April or May are likely stragglers or non-breeding individuals.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in New England during summer months, as the species is busy breeding in northern regions. Any summer sightings would be exceptional and worth reporting to local birding groups.
seasonality.fall: The first returning Common Gulls begin arriving in October, often in juvenile plumage with brownish markings. Peak migration occurs in November as birds settle into winter territories.
seasonality.winter: Most reliable season to find Common Gulls in New England, when they're in clean adult winter plumage. Look for them from December through February mixed with other gull species along the coast.

funFact: Common Gulls are surprisingly intelligent tool users that have been observed dropping shellfish from great heights onto rocks to crack them open, then carefully timing their descent to grab the meal before other gulls can steal it.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Ring-billed Gulls, but Common Gulls lack the distinctive black ring around the bill and have yellow-green (not yellow) legs and bill. Remember: 'Ring-billed has the ring, Common Gull has the clean green.'
contextualKnowledge: The Common Gull was formerly lumped together with North America's Short-billed Gull (which breeds in Alaska and western Canada) as a single species called the Mew Gull. Birdwatchers should be aware that older field guides may still use the name Mew Gull, and some identification features described for 'Mew Gulls' in older sources actually apply to the Short-billed Gull rather than the Common Gull.
compareHints: Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression. Compared to Ring-billed Gulls, Common Gulls are slightly larger with yellow-green (not bright yellow) bills that lack any dark ring, and they have a more rounded head shape. The bill and leg color coordination in Common Gulls is distinctive among New England's regular gull species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
